entries.title: Brazil ex-President Jair Bolsonaro taken to hospital over abdominal pain
entries.summary: Jair Bolsonaro has been hospitalized in Brasilia with intestinal obstruction. The former far-right Brazilian leader is receiving pain medications, his son Carlos said.
entries.content:
Brazil

Brazil ex-President Bolsonaro taken to hospital over abdominal pain

November 21, 2026

Jair Bolsonaro has been hospitalized in Brasilia with intestinal obstruction. The former far-right Brazilian leader is receiving pain medications, his son Carlos said.

Convicted former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest over a coup attempt, has been hospitalized with abdominal pain.

Bolsonaro's son Carlos wrote on X that the former far-right leader was taken to the hospital on Friday and was found to have "a near-complete intestinal obstruction."

The DF Star Hospital in Brasília said that Bolsonaro was suffering from "abdominal distension" and was being examined.

Bolsonaro's history of hospitalizations

​Bolsonaro, who is 71 years old, ‌has undergone several hospitalizations and surgeries since he was stabbed in the abdomen on the campaign trail for the 2018 elections.

"He is being given medication for pain and an initial attempt to reverse the condition without the need for invasive intervention," Carlos said.

Son blames house arrest for Bolsonaro's health issues

Bolsonaro was in power from 2019 to ​2022. He was convicted last year for plotting a coup after his defeat to current President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in the 2022 election but claims being the victim of a left-wing judicial witch hunt.

Bolsonaro was placed under humanitarian house arrest on medical grounds.

Carlos on Friday railed against his father's detention, which he blamed for Bolsonaro's current health problems.

Carlos said that the senior Bolsonaro's health was "deteriorating every day in prison due to his lack of mobility" and what he called "the psychological torture he suffers daily."

Another one of Bolsonaro's sons, Flavio Bolsonaro, recently lost the October presidential election to incumbent President Lula. Flavio Bolsonaro left Brazil after the vote and now resides in Florida.

entries.title: UK anti-migrant activist jailed for slashing Channel dinghy
entries.summary: Daniel Thomas, known as "Danny Tommo," slashed a dinghy with a knife while a French rescue worker was on board. The incident was livestreamed to a large social media audience amid growing tensions over migrant crossings.
entries.content:
November 21, 2026

Daniel Thomas, known as "Danny Tommo," slashed a dinghy with a knife while a French rescue worker was on board. The incident was livestreamed to a large social media audience amid growing tensions over migrant crossings.

A British anti-migrant activist has been sentenced to 15 months in prison for slashing a dinghy used by migrants crossing the English Channel while a French rescue worker was still on board.

Daniel Thomas, 37, also known as "Danny Tommo," pleaded guilty to criminal damage earlier this month. He was sentenced on Friday at Portsmouth Crown Court in southern England.

The activist, who founded the anti-immigration group Patriot Platform, livestreamed the September 22 incident on social media, where it was watched by a large audience.

What happened during the English Channel incident?

Thomas had followed an inflatable boat carrying dozens of migrants across the Channel on September 22.

After the migrants were transferred to another vessel and taken ashore, Thomas approached the empty dinghy, which a French rescue worker had boarded.

Video footage showed him repeatedly stabbing the boat with a knife. Judge James Newton-Price said he counted eight cuts.

During the livestream, Thomas could be heard saying "this is what needs to happen."

He also shouted "get off the boat, you've got time to get off the boat ... take them back, no more of these," according to prosecutor Joel Smith.

Newton-Price accepted that there was "no immediate danger" to the rescue worker. However, he said Thomas' aggressive behavior would have been highly alarming.

What did the judge say about Danny Tommo's actions?

Sentencing Thomas, Newton-Price said his actions amounted to "flagrant interference and a deliberate disruption" of the legitimate activities of British and French authorities in the Channel.

The judge highlighted the work of Britain's Border Force, Coastguard and volunteers from the Royal National Lifeboat Institution (RNLI).

"They do necessary, highly sensitive and difficult jobs, and which should not be disrupted by a publicity-seeker slashing with a knife a boat they were attempting to recover," he said.

Thomas appeared by videolink from a prison in Winchester, southern England, where he has been held since late September after being denied bail.

He reportedly held his head in his hands when the sentence was announced.

Under current UK sentencing rules, Thomas may serve only a third of his 15-month sentence, including time already spent in custody.

The court also heard that he had five previous convictions, including one for kidnapping in 2016.

Who is Danny Tommo and what is Patriot Platform?

Thomas is a longtime ally of prominent far-right activist Tommy Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon.

He has built a large online following and founded Patriot Platform, a group campaigning against migrants arriving in Britain in small boats.

Thomas gained prominence earlier this year by leading confrontational anti-migrant demonstrations in Portsmouth and the southeastern port of Dover.

Hundreds of protesters, many dressed in black and wearing face coverings, blocked roads and clashed with police.

The demonstrations have increasingly targeted police officers and rescue workers involved in responding to migrant boats arriving on British shores.

The UK government has condemned the protesters' "intimidating and thuggish behavior."

Thomas is also due to stand trial in London next June over several alleged offenses, including entering a restricted zone at a migrant processing center in Dover in March.

How many migrants cross the English Channel?

Successive British governments have struggled to stop migrants from making the dangerous journey across the English Channel, one of the world's busiest shipping lanes.

More than 41,000 people crossed the Channel in small boats last year.

Although the number of arrivals has since fallen, the crossings remain a major political issue in Britain.

Right-wing opposition parties and anti-immigration campaigners have continued to demand tougher measures to prevent migrants from reaching the country.

entries.title: US judge approves Bayer's $7.25 billion cancer settlement
entries.summary: Bayer could end years of costly lawsuits in the US over claims that its Roundup weedkiller causes cancer. Tens of thousands of people could now receive compensation, although some lawyers say the payments are too low.
entries.content:
November 21, 2026

Bayer could end years of costly lawsuits in the US over claims that its Roundup weedkiller causes cancer. Tens of thousands of people could now receive compensation, although some lawyers say the payments are too low.

A US judge on Friday approved German chemical giant Bayer's $7.25 billion (€6.60 billion) settlement of lawsuits claiming its Roundup weedkiller causes cancer.

Judge Timothy Boyer in the US state of Missouri ruled that the agreement was "fair, reasonable, and adequate."

The decision could help Bayer end years of costly legal battles over Roundup, which the company acquired when it bought US weedkiller producer Monsanto in 2018.

"The court's final approval is a decisive milestone in the company's strategy to mitigate the risks of both pending and future Roundup litigation," Bayer CEO Bill Anderson said.

The ruling could still be appealed.

How much money will Roundup cancer patients receive?

The agreement covers tens of thousands of people who say they developed non-Hodgkin lymphoma, a type of blood cancer, after using Roundup.

It also covers people who may be diagnosed with the disease in the future after previous exposure to the weedkiller.

Bayer will pay up to $7.25 billion into a special fund over the next 21 years.

Individual payments are expected to average between $10,000 and $165,000. The amount will depend on factors including the patient's age, the severity of the illness and how long they were exposed to Roundup.

Some lawyers representing cancer patients have criticized the payments as too low.

But the judge rejected their objections, saying that further delays could leave seriously ill patients waiting years for compensation.

Christopher Seeger, a lawyer representing cancer patients, welcomed the decision.

"Today's final approval order delivers guaranteed compensation to Roundup cancer victims who have waited more than a decade for justice," he said.

Why has it become harder to sue Bayer over Roundup?

The settlement follows a major victory for Bayer at the US Supreme Court in June.

The court ruled that Bayer could not be sued under state laws for failing to put cancer warnings on Roundup packaging.

The judges argued that US federal rules did not require such warnings and that individual states could not impose additional labeling requirements.

The decision made it much harder for cancer patients to win lawsuits against Bayer.

In October, a Missouri jury also ruled in Bayer's favor in a separate Roundup cancer case.

However, some legal battles continue. Around 200 cases are still being fought in federal courts outside the new settlement, according to Bayer.

How much have the Roundup lawsuits cost Bayer?

Monsanto introduced Roundup in 1974. Its main ingredient, glyphosate, became one of the world's most widely used weedkillers.

Farmers use Roundup to kill weeds without damaging crops that have been genetically modified to survive the chemical. It has also been widely used in private gardens and on lawns.

Bayer inherited the legal problems surrounding Roundup when it bought Monsanto for $63 billion in 2018.

Since then, around 200,000 claims have been made against Bayer by people who believe the weedkiller caused their cancer.

The company already agreed to a $10.9 billion settlement in 2020. However, it failed to secure approval for a separate agreement covering future cases.

Some lawsuits have resulted in huge payouts, including a $2.1 billion award to plaintiffs in Georgia.

Bayer has already set aside $16 billion for Roundup-related legal costs. Its shares have fallen by 46% since the Monsanto takeover.

The company has also removed glyphosate from newer versions of Roundup sold to private consumers in the United States.

Does Roundup really cause cancer?

Scientists and regulators disagree about whether glyphosate causes cancer.

In 2015, the World Health Organization's cancer research agency classified the chemical as "probably carcinogenic" to humans.

However, the US Environmental Protection Agency says glyphosate is unlikely to cause cancer when used as directed.

Bayer has repeatedly denied that Roundup causes cancer, pointing to scientific studies and regulatory approvals.

The debate intensified last year when a major scientific study that had supported Roundup's safety for decades was withdrawn.

The journal that published it cited serious problems, including missing cancer research and previously undisclosed involvement by Monsanto employees.

The withdrawal raised further questions about the influence of chemical companies on scientific research.

entries.title: Russian ornithologist jailed over small donations to Navalny's foundation
entries.summary: Sofia Rosenfeld has devoted her life to studying Arctic birds. A Russian court sentenced her to 3.5 years in a penal colony over donations to Navalny's foundation. Friends and family are fighting for her release.
entries.content:
Russian Federation

Russian ornithologist jailed over donation to Navalny foundation

November 20, 2026

Sofia Rosenfeld has devoted her life to studying Arctic birds. A Russian court sentenced her to 3.5 years in a penal colony over donations to Navalny's foundation. Friends and family are fighting for her release.

Boris Rosenfeld shows DW a photo of him with his daughter Sofia and can't hold back tears. "This was the last time we saw her. Then she left for Moscow, and this whole case began," he says.

Helives in Israel, while Sofia is in Russia. For more than a month now, she has been behind bars on charges of financing extremism. The case goes back to two donations totaling 2,000 rubles (about $30) to the late opposition politician Alexei Navalny'sAnti-Corruption Foundation (FBK), which the Russian authorities have since designated as extremist.  

On October 7, a court in Moscow sentenced Rosenfeld to three and a half years in a penal colony.

A biologist who dedicated her life to Arctic birds

Rosenfeld is a prominent ornithologist who has devoted her life to studying and protecting Arcticbirds. "Sofia was an avid young naturalist from childhood. She loved birds, horses and dogs," her father said as he leafed through a photo album. 

Sofia was a teenager when the family moved to Israel but she returned to Russia a few years later and now holds both Russian and Israeli citizenship.

She studied biology at Moscow State University and developed a significant scientific career in Russia. Her colleague, Alexandra Panyutina, who now also lives in Israel, explained that Rosenfeld was devoted to her work from an early age.

"Birds and the Arctic are the defining passions of her life," she said.

Rosenfeld was among the first Russian researchers to develop a systematic approach to monitoring migratory bird populations. To support her research, she even developed a special aircraft.

"They could fly at almost the same speed as the birds and observe them from a low altitude," says Dmitry (name changed), a colleague of Rosenfeld's. "It quickly became clear that this was a unique method."

Protecting birds in Russia and beyond

Rosenfeld is considered to be one of the leading figures in Russian ornithology. Her work has extended well beyond Russia and she has been deeply involved in international research projects. In the field of migratory bird conservation, cross-border cooperation is essential.

Helmut Kruckenberg, the head of the German Institute for Wetlands and Waterbird Research (IWWR), said Rosenfeld was highly respected within the international scientific community.

"She has done an enormous amount for nature conservation and for the protection of Siberian and Arctic species," he said. "What is happening to her is simply beyond comprehension for us."

More than 225 cases over donations to FBK across Russia

In the summer of 2021, when Russian authorities designated Alexei Navalny's Anti-Corruption Foundation, also known as FBK, as an extremist organization, Rosenfeld was on a remote Arctic expedition without a phone or access to the internet. Therefore, she did not cancel her regular donations to the FBK immediately, doing so only after her return to the Russian capital Moscow.

Her friend Olga (name changed) described Sofia as a person of absolute honesty. According to her, Rosenfeld's donations to Navalny's foundation reflected a genuine desire to fight corruption. Through her work in Russia's regions, she had seen plenty of it firsthand.

"She was never involved in political activism. Her donations were solely intended to support anti-corruption work," said her father Boris Rosenfeld. "It's unthinkable".

For him and others close to her, the sentence came as a shock. Although prosecutors had requested a five-year prison term, friends and colleagues expected that she would receive a fine at most.

There were reasons for that expectation. According to calculations by independent media outlet Mediazona, about 85% of convictions in the 225 cases involving donations to Navalny's foundation have so far resulted in non-custodial sentences. Yet Rosenfeld got three and a half years in a penal colony.

A year of court hearings and travel restrictions

Just a few months after Rosenfeld defended her doctoral dissertation in October 2025, her home was searched. She was also subject to travel restrictions. She continued to work but she had to cancel her annual summer expedition to the Arctic.

Even on the day of the sentencing, her conversations with her colleagues focused largely on science: "We discussed how the work could continue in Sofia's absence," Olga said. "But no one really believed she would end up in prison."

Leaving Russia was never an option

"The only thing we think about now is how to bring her here," Boris Rosenfeld says as he looks at the pictures from Sofia's last visit.

Friends and colleagues who spoke to DW say that his daughter never considered leaving Russia, even as the prospect of a prison sentence loomed. "Sofia would never have left. She simply can't imagine life without geese," says Dmitry.

Now, her family, friends and colleagues are campaigning to have her sentence overturned. More than 1,000 people have signed an appeal to Russia's Presidential Council for Human Rights.

Boris Rosenfeld is also hoping for support from Israel but so far Israeli consular officials have not been granted access to his daughter in detention.

The two continue to write to each other and he is trying to keep his spirits high: "She writes that she's trying to adjust to life in prison, and that it's hard," he says. "But she's a strong person."

This article was originally published in Russian.

entries.title: Repression against Iranian lawyers increases
entries.summary: At least 135 lawyers in Iran have been subjected to repressive measures over the past year. UN experts warn that this seriously jeopardizes the right of those accused to trial in a constitutional court.
entries.content:
Middle East

Iran: Lawyers increasingly under pressure

November 20, 2026

At least 135 lawyers in Iran have been subjected to repressive measures over the past year. UN experts warn that this seriously jeopardizes the right of those accused to trial in a constitutional court.

UN human rights experts have called on the Iranian authorities to end the escalating persecution of independent lawyers. They warn that limiting access to legal representation increases the risk of arbitrary detention, coerced confessions and unfair trials.

"Independent lawyers are increasingly being prosecuted and intimidated for their professional work and for defending human rights," the experts said in a statement in mid-November.

They said that between September 2025 and September 2026, at least 135 lawyers were issued with a summons, arrested, detained, suspended, dismissed or banned from traveling. In January and February 2026, 23 lawyers, including five women, were reportedly arrested after nationwide protests.

Defending the politically persecuted is becoming dangerous

A current example is the case of Amirsalar Davoudi, a human rights lawyer who was arrested in October in the central Iranian city of Isfahan, where he was defending a client in the Revolutionary Court. According to Iran Human Rights (IHRNGO), he was taken to hospital on November 9 after suffering a heart attack in custody.

"There is a long history to the persecution of and coercive measures taken against lawyers," Sina Yousefi, a 41-year-old lawyer and human rights activist, told DW.

In October 2022, Yousefi was arrested by security forces in Tabriz during the nationwide "Woman Life Freedom" protests. Later, he was sentenced to six months' imprisonment for "propaganda against the system." He has since left Iran, and now lives in the German capital Berlin.

"The pressure was already increasing on lawyers back then, because they were undertaking the defense of people who were arrested and publicly expressing their support for the demonstrators," said Yousefi. "The security services, judiciary, and criminal prosecution apparatus increasingly used targeted mechanisms to move against independent lawyers."

Even renowned and internationally known lawyers such as Nasrin Sotoudeh, who was co-awarded the Sakharov Prize in 2012, have been affected by this repression. In 2026, Sotoudeh was awarded the Vaclav Havel Human Rights Prizeafter being repeatedly arrested and imprisoned.

Yousefi said arrests and threats against lawyers working on political and human rights cases not only curtailed the rights of those accused to a defense, but also discouraged other lawyers from accepting such briefs. This, he added, compromised the fairness of trials.

Criminal proceedings have also been instigated, or other measures taken, against lawyers who undertook to represent demonstrators. Comments on social media about the violation of civil rights can also be cited as grounds for investigation and judicial proceedings.

Restrictions on the right to choose a lawyer

Yousefi also warned against tightening restrictions on a person's right to choose their own lawyer. According to the note to Article 48 of Iran's Code of Criminal Procedure, for people arrested on certain charges, access to lawyers of their own choosing is already restricted during the investigation phase. Defendants must resort to lawyers approved by the head of the judiciary. In some cases, even these lawyers are not granted access to all the files and evidence.

According to Yousefi, in many cases in which charges have been brought against demonstrators, lawyers have only been granted access to the files "when the preliminary investigations have been concluded and the evidence for the prosecution has been gathered — including confessions made during their imprisonment." Even then, he said, "their access to the records is limited and they have little time to prepare the defense."

"In many cases," Yousefi added, "the judges ascribe greater importance to reports by security agents than to the defense. Verdicts are handed down predominantly on the basis of this."

Shabnam Moinipour, the program director at the Center for Supporters of Human Rights (CSHR) in the UK, sees the independence of the bar as a fundamental precondition for the effective defense of citizens. The organization monitors the situation of lawyers in Iran, documenting violations of their rights, and following up at an international level.

"A lawyer must be able to call into question the charges brought by the public prosecutor and the credibility of the security agencies' reports without fear of criminal prosecution," Moinipour told DW. "Because when a lawyer's freedom and professional activity are threatened, their client's right to defense is impaired."

Fear and self-censorship among lawyers

In Moinipour's view, when the decision as to which lawyers are approved is made by the most senior representative of the same court authority, it raises serious questions about the independence of the bar.

"This restriction has psychological as well as legal consequences," she stressed. "For the accused, it may reinforce a sense of being unprotected, as well as feelings of fear and mistrust. It can also prevent them from disclosing details of threats, torture, and illegal behavior."

Moinipour considers this practice incompatible with Iran's obligations as a member of the UN Human Rights Committee. International law stipulates that people must have immediate access to a lawyer of their own choosing, be able to communicate with them in confidence and be supplied with sufficient means to mount a defense.

Referring to a joint report by the Tehran-based Defenders of Human Rights Center and the International Bar Association's Human Rights Institute (IBAHRI), as well as the recent statement by UN human rights experts, Moinipour said: "Even without mass arrests, the actions taken against a limited number of lawyers can send a threatening message to others and restrict their professional activity. This phenomenon is described as a chilling or deterrent effect."

However, Moinipour stressed that, despite this pressure, "many lawyers in Iran continue to defend the rights of their clients and accept the risk of arrest, criminal prosecution, and professional restrictions. In doing so, they are prepared, if necessary, to pay a high price for this resistance."

This article was originally written in Persian.

entries.title: At COP31, conflict over climate science slows action on global warming
entries.summary: Attacks on climate science and disinformation risk delaying key measures at COP31 in Antalya. As the UN climate talks draw to a close, how will that affect efforts to come to an agreement?
entries.content:
Published November 20, 2026last updated November 20, 2026

Attacks on climate science and disinformation risk delaying key measures at COP31 in Antalya. As the UN climate talks draw to a close, how will that affect efforts to come to an agreement?

The annual UN climate conference is the place where countries negotiate the world's plans to limit global warming and adapt to its consequences — and who will pay for climate action as well as damage from storms, floods and droughts. 

But this year at COP31 in Antalya, an ongoing dispute over the timing of a key assessment of global warming is risking the scientific foundations of global climate action, say observers. 

"We are extremely concerned about the situation," said a diplomat with the European delegation who could not speak on the record, adding that it came down to the future of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), the world's leading body of climate scientists.

The IPCC's scientific assessments, published every six to seven years, provide the basis for major international climate agreements, including the 2015 Paris Agreement. The IPCC began evaluating the latest climate science in 1988 and its most recent report was published in 2023. 

Researchers should have actually already started work on the next edition but the last plenary session was put on hold in October at the urging of Russia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and Kenya.

"The IPCC finds itself in a difficult situation," a spokesperson from the German Environment Ministry told DW at COP. "We stand ready to help resolve this issue, so that the panel can continue its work. To that end, we are holding many discussions with various countries to explore possible solutions."

2028 climate report card risks delay

At the core of the dispute is the question of whether future UN climate talks base their negotiations on the latest scientific knowledge — or not.

That's especially relevant for the next "global stocktake," due in 2028, a report card on the world's climate efforts, which will shape action plans for countries around the world to lower planet-heating greenhouse gas emissions.

The European Union, Brazil, the United Kingdom, small island states and several other countries especially at risk of the effects of climate change have called for the IPCC's seventh assessment report to be published in 2028, so it can be used to inform next steps for climate action. The report cover climate protection and impact.

"It's much more difficult without these scientific reports. Otherwise, we're just talking to ourselves or relying on information that's no longer current," said a delegation source.

But Russia, Iran, India and Saudi Arabia want the IPCC report postponed until 2029, after the global stocktake.

The official reason: the tight timeline would be detrimental to the quality of the research, and could hinder the participation of researchers and governments representing developing countries.

Disagreements over budget issues have also held up the IPCC's work. Among other expenses, the funds are used to pay the travel arrangements for the hundreds of volunteer scientists, especially those from poorer countries, to attend the IPCC sessions.

"No budget means no more IPCC," said a member from another delegation, also speaking on condition of anonymity.

It hasn't come to that point yet, but without planning certainty the whole process risks being delayed — along with the climate negotiations that depend on this knowledge.

Researchers with the IPCC, however, have said the timeline is attainable.

"We have no time to lose," said an open letter released in October signed by more than 100 researchers from 36 countries — including India and China. "We stand committed to continue working to deliver the [seventh assessment report] in a manner that is rigorous, timely and inclusive."

But while the dispute over the timeline won't alter the scientific findings themselves, it could delay their political impact.

EU stresses need to 'protect the integrity of climate science'

In its pre-COP communications, France accused the countries delaying the report's publication schedule of attempting to "obstruct science in order to lower the ambition of the global stocktake."

The IPCC isn't a stranger to attempts at political persuasion: At past climate conferences, delegates from many countries have regularly negotiated the exact phrasing of the summary reports intended for policymakers.

Speaking at COP31 on November 17, EU Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra said it was "fundamental to protect the integrity of climate science and the role of the IPCC as the source of best available science."

Although there is no vote on the IPCC at COP31, it's possible that its significance and a timeline for the next report will be included in the final declaration of the climate talks, expected this weekend.

Disinformation hindering climate action

The IPCC has been warning for years that disinformation is hindering global climate action. And the struggle for information and control over the narrative in Antalya hasn't just been limited to the IPCC.

This was apparent in a document DW obtained that had been sent anonymously to several less wealthy countries' delegations in the run-up to COP31.

It claimed to explain the nature of Turkey's proposed goals for boosting electrification to 35% by 2035, but went on to misrepresent several core details of the plans to make them seem less appealing to developing countries than they are in reality.

At least two countries confirmed to DW that they had received the document. It did not state where it hailed from and was labeled as an "equity assessment."

The presentation portrays electrification as a business venture undertaken by wealthy countries at the expense of poorer nations. The International Energy Agency, however, has calculated that developing countries could save around $100 billion (€90 billion) in fossil fuel imports by 2035 through electrification.

The presentation also gives the impression that all countries must meet fixed electrification targets. In fact, according to the UN, the 35% target represents a global goal, with individual countries free to determine their own national pathways.

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: COP31: UN Climate summit enters final phase with no deal in sight
entries.summary: After nearly two weeks of negotiations, countries remain divided on how to fight global warming. A new draft declaration doesn't mention the phaseout of fossil fuels, the main drivers of climate change. DW has more.
entries.content:
Published November 20, 2026last updated November 21, 2026

After nearly two weeks of negotiations, countries remain divided on how to fight global warming. A new draft declaration doesn't mention the phaseout of fossil fuels, the main drivers of climate change. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Diplomats and delegates from nearly 200 countries are meeting in Antalya, Turkey

  • A new draft deal omits any mention of how to phase out fossil fuels, in what campaigners call a step 'backwards' and a 'glaring regression'

  • Like in previous years, the climate summit is likely to be extended until a consensus is reached

These are the major developments from the closing phase of the UN's COP31 Climate Summit in Antalya, Turkey, on Friday, November 20 and Saturday, November 21:

Skip next section COP31 talks go on — we're taking a break

COP31 talks go on — we're taking a break

The UN climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, has gone into overtime, with countries still divided over key issues, including fossil fuels and climate financing.

The talks were scheduled to end on Friday evening, but negotiators have yet to reach an agreement. Germany and several other countries are pushing for a clear commitment to phase out fossil fuels, while poorer nations are demanding more concrete financial support to cope with climate change.

Negotiations are expected to continue into the weekend. We are pausing our live coverage for now and will bring you further updates as talks progress.

Skip next section WATCH — Turkey's beaches are becoming too hot for sea turtles

WATCH — Turkey's beaches are becoming too hot for sea turtles

While Turkey hosts COP31 in Antalya, a growing climate threat is unfolding on its Mediterranean beaches. Rising sand temperatures are causing most newly hatched sea turtles to be born female, raising concerns about the long-term survival of local populations.

Conservationists warn that climate change, combined with pollution, coastal development and fishing-related injuries, is putting increasing pressure on the species.

DW correspondent Julia Hahn follows the people working to protect Turkey's iconic loggerhead turtles and shows how the climate crisis is already affecting wildlife far beyond the COP31 conference halls.

Skip next section WATCH — COP climate summit under scrutiny over fossil fuel influence

WATCH — COP climate summit under scrutiny over fossil fuel influence

The UN climate summit in Antalya is drawing criticism from activists and campaigners who question whether global climate talks can deliver meaningful change while fossil fuel interests remain influential. Turkey and Australia, both under scrutiny for their energy policies, are leading this year's conference.

Activists, including Greta Thunberg, argue COP summits have become increasingly ineffective, while others defend them as a vital space to pressure governments. Climate policy experts say the talks have helped reduce projected warming, but stress that real progress depends on action taken by countries between summits, not just agreements reached at them.

Skip next section WATCH — Maldives environment minister: 'We are not going to live in the dark'

WATCH — Maldives environment minister: 'We are not going to live in the dark'

For the Maldives, climate change is already affecting everyday life. Heavy rainfall has forced people from their homes, warmer oceans are damaging coral reefs, and changes in fish stocks are putting pressure on the country's fishing industry. Rising sea levels pose another threat to the low-lying island nation. Meanwhile, global greenhouse gas emissions continue to rise, despite more than three decades of international climate negotiations.

At COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, the Maldives' climate minister Ali Sharif discusses why progress has been so slow, what really happens during climate negotiations, and why moving away from fossil fuels is not as straightforward as it might seem.

For island nations like the Maldives, switching to renewable energy comes with practical and financial challenges. So what would it take to accelerate the transition? And can the UN climate process still deliver meaningful results?

Skip next section COP32 hosts Ethiopia call the conferences a relay, not a single race

COP32 hosts Ethiopia call the conferences a relay, not a single race

The hosts of next year's COP, Ethiopia, found a nationally tailored sporting metaphor to sum up the difficult, ongoing, sometimes tortuous process that the global environmental meetings can prove to be.

Speaking at the end of Friday's plenary to confirm Addis Ababa's intentions to host next year's summit, Gedion Timothewos, the foreign minister and upcoming president of COP32, made reference to Ethiopia's longstanding success in endurance running in track and field.

Referring to the COP process as a marathon, not a sprint, Timothewos said the country was looking forward to picking up the baton from Turkey and leading the next leg of the relay, taking the ongoing process forward into 2027.

His comments came during a late-night plenary session, but more talks are still expected in Antalya.

Skip next section Late-night plenary session convenes after delay

Late-night plenary session convenes after delay

Shortly after 9 p.m. local time in Antalya, delegates gathered for a plenary session, well past the official closing time.

The Turkish presidency's opening address was partly drowned out by a protester shouting objections in English such as "you are killing the future," and gaining applause within the chamber.

"We've been negotiating for days to find the common ground," COP31 President Murat Kurum, Turkey's environment minister, told the plenary. He hailed the progress made and said the world "waits for good news from this room."

But the plenary session noted how several of the more ambitious aspects of a political declaration remained incomplete, with no agreement yet reached at the summit.

Several national delegates spoke during the plenary to bemoan the elusive progress or even backsliding during the two weeks of negotiations.

The evening's session, however, has been dealing with technical issues, and the possibility that discussions continue into the weekend remains.

Skip next section IN DEPTH — Climate science disputes and disinformation hinder action at COP

IN DEPTH — Climate science disputes and disinformation hinder action at COP

Attacks on climate science and disinformation risk delaying key measures at COP31 in Antalya. As the UN climate talks draw to a close, how will that affect efforts to come to an agreement?

The UN's IPCC should have already started work on its next series of multi-year scientific assessments on climate change's progress, but the process is on hold at the urging of countries including fossil fuel-producing giants Russia, Saudi Arabia and Iran.

Read Tim Schauenberg's full report on this obstruction to climate research and other similar issues complicating COP31 here. 

Skip next section IN DEPTH — US is strong at climate talks despite Trump no-show

IN DEPTH — US is strong at climate talks despite Trump no-show

The US government is snubbing UN climate talks in Turkey. That's prompted a delegation of American lawmakers, mayors and governors to make the trip instead, aiming to show that climate action in the US is alive and well.

Head over to this report to learn more about who is representing the US at the summit, even if President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly dismissed global warming as a "hoax", didn't send a formal delegation for the second year in a row.

Skip next section IN DEPTH — Uganda minister at COP31: 'We need a just transition'

IN DEPTH — Uganda minister at COP31: 'We need a just transition'

Funding from wealthy countries to help deal with the impacts of climate change hasn't materialized, says Uganda's environment minister. The East African country is hoping oil and carbon credits will help boost finances.

Learn more about what Uganda's environment minister Beatrice Atim Anywar said about climate financing in this report.

Skip next section Activist Menotti: Europe has 'learned a few of the Trump tactics'

Activist Menotti: Europe has 'learned a few of the Trump tactics'

Veteran climate justice advocate Victor Menotti of the Demand Climate Justice NGO told DW that European governments appeared to be copying US President Donald Trump's negotiating playbook at COP this year.

"We know the US isn't here, but we can see that Germany and other European governments have learned a few of the Trump tactics, maybe in the trade disputes with the US," Menotti said. "And we see them applying here in Antalya, where it's like: Don't admit to anything. Try to dilute your responsibilities. Weaken whatever obligations you have. And then take even more."

He argued these countries were also expecting unreasonable or unfeasible commitments from developing countries, for instance restrictions on what they can spend money on and obligations to report on their expenditures.

"Germany is subsidizing quite a bit of coal still and fossil fuels, LNG expansion infrastructure," he said, arguing that wealthier countries' energy spending also had room for improvement.

"We need the North to act first," Menotti said. "The deal from Paris, the deal from Rio 30 years ago, is that the North will lead. But yet we see too much bullying of the global South and not enough leadership like they agreed to."

Skip next section Talks formally enter overtime as scheduled close elapses

Talks formally enter overtime as scheduled close elapses

You can cross off another box on your COP31 bingo cards, dear readers.

As of the top of this hour, the session has officially gone past its scheduled end time of 1500 GMT/UTC on Friday, or 6 p.m. local time on site in Turkey.

This is something of an annual tradition at COP summits, which are always scheduled to finish at the end of a working week but also almost invariably run into the closing weekend. Delegates and members of the media tend to book their travel plans with this in mind.

Skip next section 'Electrification': What to know about the revised draft declaration

'Electrification': What to know about the revised draft declaration

The revised draft declaration, which critics have slammed as "watered down" due to the omission of fossil fuels, highlights the "electrification" of the global economy as a central pillar of the energy transition.

"Electrification is the key to transitioning away from fossil fuels," Australian Climate Minister Chris Bowen told reporters.

What are the key points to know about the "35-by-35" electrification target?

  • The draft wants to increase electricity's share of global energy use from 23% to 35% by 2035
  • The draft highlights electrification as a way to cut emissions and boost energy security — while omitting prior mentions of fossil fuels
  • It aims to shift more transport, heating, cooling and industrial activity onto electricity, allowing those sectors to be powered by renewables such as wind, solar and hydro power, rather than by burning coal, oil or gas

But the text does not specify what energy sources would supply the electricity. Some countries are demanding that the text call for "clean" electrification to clearly favor renewable sources over coal, oil or gas.

Bowen, who has been trying to secure compromises, pledged to continue working over the "coming hours, for as long as it takes, to get the job done."

"People have strong views of course — I am not stepping away from that. But no one has said to me let's give up and go home," Bowen said.

Skip next section Climate Action Network blames rich nations for 'worst COP ever'

Climate Action Network blames rich nations for 'worst COP ever'

The Climate Action Network (CAN), a global network of over 2,500 civil society organizations, has accused wealthy developed nations, led by the EU, "of blocking every track" towards a substantive agreement on fighting climate change and curbing fossil fuel use.

At its final press conference of the summit, CAN executive director Tasneem Essop said the group was "rejecting what is currently on the table."

"There is nothing (...) that protects people or addresses the priorities of the Global South. In fact, the opposite is true. The current text has opened the door to the most harmful and dangerous options of any COP so far," Essop said.

She pointed out that this year's COP had the highest ever number of lobbyists for fossil fuels, for AI, for CCUS (Carbon Capture, Utilization, and Storage) and for CDR (Carbon Dioxide Removal), which only represent corporate interests and do not have the interests of the people from developing nations who are most at risk from global warming in mind.

"What we’re leaving this COP with is decisions made to promote the interests of those corporations making profits from the destruction of people," Essop said.

Mohamed Adow from Power Shift Africa, which is also part of CAN, said: "The COP Presidents want to tell us this has been a great COP. Well, I can tell you without any doubt that this has been the worst COP ever.

"Overseeing a failing COP is bad enough, but trying to sell it as a success rubs salt into the wounds of those people who need it to deliver."

Adow cautioned that communities that live with the constant threat of drought, floods and failed harvests were "promised action."

"They cannot survive on an annual renewal of promises," Adow said.

He laid the blame squarely with the world's most developed nations: "They demand action from developing countries, then block public finance, block Just Transition, block climate finance, and they expect ambition. You cannot keep your foot on the brake and complain that countries are not moving fast enough."

Skip next section 'Are you serious?' Youth climate activist questions rich nations' commitment

'Are you serious?' Youth climate activist questions rich nations' commitment

Xiye Bastida, a New York-based youth activist from Mexico, spoke to DW's Katharina Schantz to describe her frustration over the lack of progress and ambition on display at this year's COP Summit, which is the seventh the 24-year-old has attended.

Bastida, who has played a leading role in the Fridays for Future climate movement in New York, said she did not think she "could be more disappointed" at how climate targets are "being rolled back."

"This is really the time of reckoning," Bastida said.

She explained that she had changed her flight plans to be able to stay until the end, because she feels "we have to be here. We at least to be witnesses of how they're taking things away."

Bastida pointed to the hypocrisy from wealthy nations, who have blamed some from the Global South for not wanting the summit's joint declaration to mention fossil fuels.

"But they (the Global North) are the ones not bringing the money, and they're the ones who are not bringing the ambition.

"And they want to show themselves as the leaders. But if you want to mention fossil fuels so bad, where's the money for the transition? Where are the roadmaps?

"Are you serious?" Bastida concluded.

Skip next section 'We fear the last couple of weeks will be just a talk show': Sierra Leone spokesperson tells DW

'We fear the last couple of weeks will be just a talk show': Sierra Leone spokesperson tells DW

The new draft declaration, which, as we've reported, has been panned by the EU and civil society, has also disappointed some of the world's least developed countries (LDCs) that are most vulnerable to climate change.

The LDC Group, which comprises 44 of the world's least wealthy nations, came into this year's COP summit hoping for stronger climate action than what has been achieved so far.

"It’s a moment of anticipation," Lamin Sheriff, a press attache for the Sierra Leone government, told DW's Katharina Schantz.

"Ministers from LDCs have requests on the table for the presidency. So whilst they wait on what the outcome would be, everybody is waiting patiently. So the moment is really: we are hopeful for the future, but we are also worried because if proper care is not taken, all what we have debated about here in the last couple of weeks will just be a talk show (…) We can't do anything at the moment."

entries.title: Has the 'Parthenon puzzle' been solved? The long quest to reassemble lost eastern pediment
entries.summary: The depiction of the birth of the goddess Athena above the Parthenon's entrance is considered a masterpiece of ancient art. Now, a German research team has pieced together all the surviving fragments.
entries.content:
November 20, 2026

The depiction of the birth of the goddess Athena above the Parthenon's entrance is considered a masterpiece of ancient art. Now, a German research team has pieced together all the surviving fragments.

The 2,500-year-old Parthenon is ancient Greece's most important temple and is regarded as one of the greatest masterpieces of the High Classical period of Greek art.

Dedicated to Athena, the city's patron goddess, it towers over Athens from its position on the Acropolis — a powerful symbol of the city's importance.

The Parthenon had a lasting influence on Western ideas of humanity and art. The sculptures adorning its pediments, created under the direction of the legendary sculptor Phidias, are considered unparalleled examples of proportion and grace. They have influenced artists from ancient Rome through Neoclassicism to the modern era.

'Very confident we've solved the mystery'

The east pediment above the temple entrance depicted the birth of the goddess Athena from the head of her father Zeus, surrounded by the Olympian gods. A total of 39 figures adorned the roughly 29-meter-long work of art. At its center stood a colossal Zeus figure, measuring 3.8 meters in height.

For centuries, scholars have puzzled over exactly what the arrangement looked like, as the pediment was destroyed during the Christianization of Greece.

But now there has been a breakthrough.

After decades of painstaking detective work and with the help of modern technology, archaeologist Vinzenz Brinkmann and his team have managed to piece together all the surviving fragments of the Parthenon's east pediment.

Brinkmann heads the Antiquities and Asia department at Frankfurt's Liebieghaus sculpture collection. "We're very, very confident that we've solved the mystery," he told DW.

The results are now on display in an exhibition at the Liebieghaus titled "Athena, the Stage is Yours: The Parthenon Puzzle."

Only around 20% of the original marble sculpture's volume is known to have survived. The fragments are scattered across various European museums, with most located in Athens. The British Museum also holds numerous pieces.

Brinkmann and his wife, Ulrike Koch-Brinkmann, have spent more than 40 years working on this ancient puzzle, with so many of its pieces missing.

And they were far from the first to attempt it: "Already in the 19th century, many scholars studied the subject and developed well-founded theories based on their deep knowledge of ancient sources," Brinkmann explains.

In 1910, a study documenting the many fragments held by the British Museum was published. The research team was able to build on that earlier work, but progress remained slow for years.

Then, in 2014, a visit to the Hermitage Museum in St. Petersburg provided Brinkmann with a crucial clue. There, he encountered a Roman sarcophagus featuring a relief of Athena's birth. "That's when it suddenly clicked: They're all there!"

Nine such sarcophagi are known to exist, almost all of them in Rome. Each depicts a different section of the Parthenon's east pediment.

Brinkmann emphasizes that other scholars had already noticed this connection in the 19th century. "But we really seized on the idea and never let go."

A handy tool: the iPhone

The researchers also benefited from 21st-century technology: 3D scanners and printers. Brinkmann and his team visited numerous destinations to examine around 60 original fragments at different locations — traveling light. An iPhone was all they needed to scan the pieces.

Digitally fitting the fragments together led to another important discovery. "We know these figures we're putting together!" Brinkmann recalls thinking at the time.

The Romans had repeatedly made individual copies of all the sculptures from the pediment. "These copies matched the fragments perfectly. Suddenly, we found ourselves surrounded by old acquaintances we had never suspected had come from the pediment." This finally enabled the researchers to reconstruct all the figures and their original arrangement.

Using a 3D printer, the team created a 4-meter-long model at a scale of 1:7.7. For the exhibition, they also produced life-size 3D prints of the most important fragments and mounted them on panels depicting the complete figures at their original size. An animation brings the reconstructed composition to life, digitally assembling the fragments to reveal how the east pediment once looked.

Alongside works from the Liebieghaus collection, the exhibition features loans from other institutions, including the Vatican Museums and the Louvre. Objects from the Acropolis Museum in Athens had originally been expected as well. But Greece withdrew its participation after learning that the British Museum was also planning to lend fragments to the Frankfurt exhibition. The Liebieghaus ultimately decided to forgo the British-owned fragments, too.

The dispute between Greece and Britain over the Parthenon sculptures

There is a reason for this controversy. Britain holds a substantial portion of the Parthenon frieze as well as fragments from both pediments.

Greek authorities have been campaigning for their return for decades.

In Britain, the 56 sections of the frieze are known as the "Elgin Marbles," named after Lord Elgin, the British ambassador to the Ottoman Empire in Constantinople.

In the early 19th century, Elgin had sculptures removed from the exterior of the Parthenon on the Acropolis in Athens. They were taken to Britain with the consent of the Ottoman Empire, which ruled Greece at the time.

Britain maintains that the sculptures were legally acquired.

Greece, however, considers them stolen.

For years, the dispute remained deadlocked. Since the Labour Party came to power in Britain, there has been some movement toward resolving it. But apparently not enough to persuade Greece to lend artworks to an exhibition in which the British Museum might also participate.

The exhibition "Athena, the Stage is Yours. The Parthenon Puzzle" runs through July 25, 2027, at the Liebieghaus in Frankfurt.

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: Germany news: Kids take to streets over school, climate and costs
entries.summary: Thousands of young people turned out across Germany demanding improvements in education, climate and affordability. Protesters say they aren't being taken seriously and will keep protesting until things change.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Kids take to streets over school, climate and costs

Published November 20, 2026last updated November 20, 2026

Thousands of young people turned out across Germany demanding improvements in education, climate and affordability. Protesters say they aren't being taken seriously and will keep protesting until things change.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

This blog is now closed. Thank you for reading.

Below, you can review a roundup of the biggest headlines in Germany from Friday, November 20: 

  • Large rallies took place across Germany with young people protesting in Berlin, Cologne, Hamburg and elsewhere
  • Young people feel politicians are not taking their concerns seriously
  • Chancellor Merz announces Qatar to invest €15 billion more in German defense tech
  • Lufthansa to reportedly slash 1,000 positions at Frankfurt and Munich hubs

Skip next section Metalworkers' union to continue one-day strikes as wage talks near

Metalworkers' union to continue one-day strikes as wage talks near

Representatives of IG Metall, Germany's largest union, said Friday that thousands of union workers at dozens of factories around the country will continue to carry out 24-hour strikes in an effort to force employers to cough up a 5% wage increase as well as job guarantees. 

Audi, BMW, Ford, Opel and Volkswagen are all in IG Metall's sights, as are shipyards in northern Germany.

Companies say they cannot afford to pay wage increases and will have to slash benefits, site upgrades and hundreds of thousands of jobs in the automotive, electrical and mechanical engineering and metal production sectors.

They are instead offering a phased increase of 1.3% for 2028 — Germany's current inflation rate is hovering around 3%.

It is the first time the union and its 3.7 million members have turned to 24-hour strikes in eight years and they are hoping the move will offer them some leverage when collective bargaining talks begin next week.

IG Metall's northern coastal representative Daniel Friedrich said Friday: "Our members stand united behind our demands. On Monday, we will continue the 24-hour strikes at more companies."

Skip next section Police in Leipzig respond to fireworks attacks with water cannon

Police in Leipzig respond to fireworks attacks with water cannon

Police in the German state of Saxony say they deployed water cannons to Leipzig and used them on individuals who repeatedly shot fireworks at officers there after a large demonstration ended.

Police say roughly 2,500 people took part in a demonstration in Leipzig organized by the group Gen Z Takes Charge, far fewer than the estimated 7,000 who joined the first of these on October 31 (see entries below).

Across Germany, some 87,000 people joined in demonstrations, according to Gen Z Takes Charge.

Skip next section Qatar to invest €15 billion more in German defense tech, says Merz

Qatar to invest €15 billion more in German defense tech, says Merz

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Friday announced that Qatari Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani had pledged €15 billion ($16.5 billion) in new German defense and technology investments. 

During a Berlin press conference with the emir, Merz said, "This strengthens both of us, particularly in future technologies such as artificial intelligence, semiconductors and aviation."

The Qatar-Germany collaboration is aimed at improving security and defense projects that also include defending against cyberattacks, with Merz saying, "We are particularly open to new partnerships in the defense industry."

That cooperation comes as both nations look to beef up defenses amid regional conflicts with global consequences. 

The chancellor and the emir also stressed the fundamental importance of diplomacy in the resolution of conflict, with the two leaders' focused largely on Iran and the Middle East — and the need to get the flow of shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz closer to pre-war levels. 

The emir called for deescalation, saying, "We are convinced that true political resolution is the only way to achieve lasting peace."

Merz added that the two agreed on the war in Ukraine, saying: "Russia must stop its time-wasting diplomatic games. Moscow has to finally sit down for real peace negotiations."

Merz was straightforward on Iran, saying Germany wants peace in the Middle East because it needs affordable energy.

He later called out Russian maritime marauding on the Black Sea, labeling it a threat to global food security.

Skip next section Germany's Sky TV won't send staff to F1 race in Qatar

Germany's Sky TV won't send staff to F1 race in Qatar

The German broadcaster Sky TV — not to be confused with the British-based Sky Sports F1 which is the largest English-language commercial F1 broadcaster — will not be sending any staff to the Formula 1 Qatar Grand Prix because of security concerns in connection with the conflict in Iran and the wider Middle East. 

Sky TV announced the move on Friday, just a week before the contentious race weekend from November 27-29.

Sky will broadcast the entire race weekend as usual, but will use global feed images and will not send any of its own staff to Lusail International Circuit.

F1 races in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia this spring were canceled as the US war with Iran was in its most active phase, with major disruptions to commercial flights. 

The season-ending double header in Qatar and then the United Arab Emirates a week later has been in serious doubt ever since. 

Nominally at least, both races are going ahead — and in all likelihood, teams will have already started dispatching equipment and personnel to the region to begin preparations by now.

Sky TV said it still planned to send a team to the season finale in Abu Dhabi, just across the Strait of Hormuz from Iran, on December 6.

But it said it continued to "monitor developments and assess the situation on an ongoing basis."

Skip next section Gen Z protesters rally around Germany

Gen Z protesters rally around Germany

Organizers of the Gen Z Takes Charge protest group spoke out about why they took to the streets again.

Co-organizer Akram Selo called on Germany's leadership to meet the young people's demands.

"Talks won't make us stop demonstrating," he told RBB-Inforadio in comments aired on Friday.

"Essentially, our demands should be addressed, and we should be given assurances. That is what needs to happen, not empty promises," Selo added.

"So far, we feel that we aren't being taken seriously at all," he said. "The way we're being treated suggests that the aim is to sideline our demands and discriminate against us by focusing on other trivial matters."

Another group, the alliance "School strike against conscription" held its own protest to demand an immediate halt to surveys about potential availability for the German Armed Forces, or Bundeswehr, that are currently non-binding and only obligatory for teenage boys.

Skip next section Merz urges Ukraine to push reforms in return for investment

Merz urges Ukraine to push reforms in return for investment

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Ukraine must ‌continue ⁠to ⁠push ahead swiftly with reforms, particularly ​on the rule of ​law and tackling ​corruption, ‌if it hopes to receive a prerequisite for further financial ‌aid and investment.

Merz made the comment at a ‌business ​summit in Berlin that was organized by the German Chamber of Industry and Commerce.

"It is now essential to press ahead with these reforms swiftly and resolutely —particularly, and I say this openly, with regard to the rule of law and corruption," Merz told attendees.

The German chancellor said that sustained reform efforts by Kyiv ​were necessary to justify long-term Western support ⁠for ​Ukraine, adding ​that Germany would ​step up ‌its backing in defense and humanitarian ​aid ⁠as Russia intensifies attacks on ⁠Ukraine's ​energy infrastructure ahead of winter.

"What we invest in Ukraine now, we will receive back many times over as dividends in the form of stability, export opportunities, joint projects, and growth," the German chancellor said.

In 2025, the two countries traded goods worth around €12 billion ($13 billion).

"Freedom and security are now unleashing forces of progress and resilience on a scale never seen before. This is precisely the stance we are now taking against the autocratic and imperialist actors of this world. We are the world of freedom," Merz added.

At home, Merz has faced increasing pressure to justify Germany's ongoing support for Ukraine. In recent regional elections, political parties opposing sending military aid have performed well.

Merz argued that Russia's war against Ukraine is an attack on democratic values everywhere.

Skip next section Germany's electricity exports rise

Germany's electricity exports rise

Germany's electricity exports rose in the first three quarters of this year, according to official data released on Friday.

According to the energy association BDEW, Germany has been a net importer of electricity since 2023.

The neighbouring countries Austria, Denmark and the Netherlands, were the most important buyers of German electricity in the first nine months of 2026.

Together, they bought about half of all German electricity exports.

The volume of German electricity exported rose by 25.5% compared with the same period last year, to 48.8 terawatt-hours, while its value increased by 51.3% to €4.3 billion ($4.7 billion). 



Electricity imports into Germany fell by 13.3% in volume, but at 49.2 terawatt-hours they remained slightly above exports.

While imported electricity cost an average of €116 per megawatt-hour, 39% more than a year earlier, exported electricity from Germany averaged only €87 per megawatt-hour, some 20.6% more than a year earlier.

With a high share of renewable energy sources, wind and solar, Germany tends to offer electricity when supply is high and prices are low, but in times of shortage it has to pay higher prices for imported electricity.

Skip next section German Finance Ministry launches dialogue on economic future

German Finance Ministry launches dialogue on economic future

Finance Ministry officials said they are launching a dialogue process, dubbed "Germany 2035," to develop proposals for the future of the country's economy.

Officials want to study how Germany can secure growth and prosperity and what that could look like in terms of fiscal policy.

Finance Minister Lars ​Klingbeil will begin the dialogue process on December ​2, when he welcomes economists from around the world to Berlin.

Additionally, think tanks, research organizations, universities and civil society groups have been asked to host workshops, which would take place in the first half of 2027.

Among 12 economic topics that the ministry seeks to explore are tax and fiscal policy, investment ⁠and ​domestic demand, industrial policy, energy ​and climate transition, foreign trade and sovereignty, and housing ​and local infrastructure.

The dialogue will culminate in a white paper, to be published in 2028, that can provide recommendations for Germany's economic future up to 2035.

Skip next section Youth protests expected in German cities

Youth protests expected in German cities

A group called "Gen Z Takes Charge" (Gen Z regelt) has called for thousands of young people to demonstrate in many German cities.

The gathering comes almost three weeks after the first major youth protests hit Germany, inspired by the protests that took place in France in the last weeks.

Those protests, which took place on October 31, saw tens of thousands take to the streets across Germany, with crowds remaining largely peaceful, although rioting broke out in several cities, including Frankfurt, later in the evening.

Among the demands of the "Gen Z Takes Charge" group are increased funding for schools, addiction support and psychotherapy, affordable living, opposition to conscription and consistent action on climate change.

Another group, the Federal Pupils' Conference, has also organized its own demonstration at the Brandenburg Gate in Berlin, with police saying that some 5,000 people have already signed up.

The pupils' conference advocates for improvements in education policy in Germany, including school renovation, school social work, relief for teachers and the inclusion of climate action in curricula.

The demonstrations are set to begin in the morning and run until late afternoon.

Skip next section President Steinmeier welcomes Emir of Qatar

President Steinmeier welcomes Emir of Qatar

President Frank-Walter Steinmeier welcomed the Emir of Qatar Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani in Berlin with military honors.

Steinmeier will also host a state banquet for the emir and his delegation in the evening. Al Thani is also expected to meet with Chancellor Friedrich Merz during the day.

The visit comes in the midst of tensions in the Middle East, with the war in Iran likely to be a critical topic in the talks between the two governments. Qatar is currently one of the mediators in the deadlocked conflict between the US and Iran.

Economic and bilateral relations are also expected to take center stage.

On Saturday, the emir will visit Germany's most populous state of North Rhine-Westphalia, where he will be greeted by its state premier Hendrik Wüst at the military section of Cologne/Bonn Konrad Adenauer Airport.

During the visit, Al Thani and North Rhine-Wesphalia leaders will hold an economic conference in the small city of Königswinter, near Bonn, where the Emir will also visit Drachenburg Castle.

Skip next section Merz to visit German-Ukrainian business forum in Berlin

Merz to visit German-Ukrainian business forum in Berlin

Following a political summit on Ukraine in Berlin yesterday, the German Chamber of Industry and Commerce (DIHK) said it would host a German-Ukrainian business forum.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz and German Economy Minister Katherina Reiche are expected to be in attendance, along with Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi, among others.

Christian Bruch, deputy chair of the Eastern Committee of the German Economy and chief executive of Siemens Energy, said German companies are committed to invest in Ukraine, despite Russia's ongoing war and were open to expand their business partnerships.

Bruch said bilateral trade was expected to rise to around €13 billion ($14.1 billion) in 2026.

Skip next section Lufthansa to slash 1,000 jobs in Frankfurt, Munich — reports

Lufthansa to slash 1,000 jobs in Frankfurt, Munich — reports

German flagship airline Lufthansa plans to cut 1,000 jobs at its airport hubs in Frankfurt and Munich, according to a company letter seen by German news agency DPA and news outlets. 

The letter was reportedly signed by Lufthansa Airlines CEO Jens Ritter and four other managers.

The timeframe of the cuts is unclear. It's also unknown whether the cuts were apart of a previously announced downsizing.

In September 2025, Lufthansa said it would slash 4000 administrative positions due to the implementation of AI and digitalization.     

Lufthansa's parent company Lufthansa Group had 67,100 employees in Germany by the end of last year. In the letter seen by news agencies, Lufthansa said financial struggles were the reason behind the planned cuts.

"Lufthansa is currently not competitive in terms of its cost structure, efficiency and productivity," the letter said, while pointing out that the company operated at a €180 million ($197 million) loss in the first nine months of this year.

In addition, Lufthansa Airlines is now in its third straight year of being unprofitable.

In regards to this year, Lufthansa has faced rising fuel costs spurred by the US-Israeli war with Iran, further complicating its financial outlook.   

Skip next section WATCH: Leaked files raise questions over Deutsche Bank's Russia ties

WATCH: Leaked files raise questions over Deutsche Bank's Russia ties

Leaked documents raise new questions about Deutsche Bank's dealings in Russia up to Moscow's invasion of Ukraine, adding to scrutiny over the bank's risk controls and past controversies.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Guten Tag and welcome to DW's daily coverage of Germany-related news on Friday. 

Lufthansa is reportedly planning on cutting jobs as the German flag carrier faces financial difficulties.

Meanwhile, youth-protests are expected across Germany and Qatari's emir is visiting Berlin, where he is expected to meet with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

Stay tuned for the latest on all this and more throughout the day from the heart of Europe.

entries.title: Ukraine updates: Russian attack 'one of largest,' Zelenskyy says
entries.summary: Ukrainian President Zelenskyy said Russia launched one of the largest aerial attacks since the invasion began. Poland accused Moscow of a "provocation," saying two missiles landed in the NATO country.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Ukraine updates: Russian attack 'one of largest,' Zelenskyy says

Published November 20, 2026last updated November 20, 2026

Ukrainian President Zelenskyy said Russia launched one of the largest aerial attacks since the invasion began. Poland accused Moscow of a "provocation," saying two missiles landed in the NATO country.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

This blog is now closed. Thank you for reading.

Below you can follow the latest updates from Russia's war in Ukraine on Friday, 20th November:

  • Zelenskyy said the Russian attack included 400 drones and more than 110 missiles, including 27 ballistic missiles
  • At least 8 people were killed and several bridges and energy facilities were hit
  • Poland called a violation of its airspace by the Russian attack an 'intentional provocation'
  • France has called for a UN Security Council meeting in light of the attacks

Skip next section France's Macron calls Russia's 'aggressive agenda' in Europe an 'irresponsible gamble'

France's Macron calls Russia's 'aggressive agenda' in Europe an 'irresponsible gamble'

French President Emmanuel Macron on Friday described Russia's actions in Ukraine and Europe as an "irresponsible gamble" that would only increase European resolve.



"By escalating its war of aggression against Ukraine and also pursuing an aggressive agenda on European soil, Russia is making an irresponsible gamble that can only further isolate it and strengthen the resolve and unity of Europeans, and of all those who want to work towards peace and stability on our continent," he wrote on X.

Macron posted his comments after Moscow hit Ukraine with massive strikes and two Russian missiles appeared to have landed in Poland.

Denmark meanwhile accused Russia of attempting to assassinate a Ukrainian rapper on its soil.

Skip next section Trump says Putin's his 'friend,' not sure if he's a friend to America

Trump says Putin's his 'friend,' not sure if he's a friend to America

US President Donald Trump has defended his admiration for Russian President Vladimir Putin while deflecting a reporter's question as to whether the Russian strongman is a friend to the United States or just the president.

"I can't speak to America" but said: "I consider him to be somebody that I have a very good relationship [with]. It's actually very good."

Trump said the two bonded over the 2016 US presidential election, which Democrats say involved Russian meddling on Trump's behalf, charges that Trump rejects as what he has branded the "Russia hoax."

The US leader also said it will be hard to end the war in Ukraine — something he said he would easily do on his first day back in office nearly two years ago — because of the animosity between Putin and Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

"It's a very hard thing to do, to be honest. You have two guys that don't know how to end it. We're trying to help them. You have two people that hate each other."

Once again, Trump also claimed, with no real world evidence, that Putin would "love to end the war" that he launched in February 2022, despite the fact that Russia launched massive attacks on neighboring Ukraine as soon as his meeting with Trump and Xi had ended.

Skip next section Trump: Swoons over relationship with Putin, won't discuss Ukraine security

At least 1,144 children were killed or injured in Ukraine during the first 10 months of 2026, the United Nations said.

UNICEF, the UN's children's agency, said that between January and October, at least 114 children were killed and 1,030 injured.

The agency said it was the highest number of casualties seen in more than 3 years.

"That is more than three children who have been killed or injured every single day" this year, said UNICEF spokeswoman Louise Wateridge.
